What is the total weight of a ten-storey reinforced concrete residential building with a 20 × 20 m footprint?
Floors, walls, columns and finishes, plus the people and furniture in the building.

For a framed building, a good first estimate is that every storey transmits roughly 10 kN, i.e. about 1 tonne, per square metre. This is what the ground has to carry, and if a raft covers the whole plan, the contact pressure is about 10 kPa per storey – about 100 kPa for ten storeys.
G + Q ≈ 10 storeys · 400 m² · 10 kN/m² = 40 000 kN
At least how deep below foundation level must you drill next to a 2.0 m wide pad footing?
Average ground conditions; the depth of the bearing stratum is not yet known.

For pad and strip footings, the investigation depth below foundation level is at least three times the footing width, and at least 6 m. The stress from the footing load still reaches this depth, and the influence depth also lies within it.
If the angle of shearing resistance of a sand increases from 30° to 35°, by what factor does the bearing capacity factor N<sub>q</sub> increase?
A difference of only 5 degrees, which can occur even between two tests.

The bearing capacity factors increase very rapidly with the friction angle. That is why a reliable value of φ′ is decisive: an error of a few degrees means far more than ten or twenty per cent in bearing resistance.
And if φ′ increases from 20° to 35°: by what factor does N<sub>γ</sub> increase?
This factor appears in the term proportional to the footing width.

N<sub>γ</sub> increases even more steeply than N<sub>q</sub>. Between a loose, low-friction soil and a dense sand there is an order of magnitude – the same footing passes comfortably on one and fails on the other.
What water pressure acts from below on the base slab of a basement 7.6 m deep if the groundwater is 3.0 m below ground level?
A two-level underground car park with a watertight diaphragm wall and base slab.

Water pressure depends only on the depth below the water table: 10 kPa per metre. 46 kPa is about 4.6 t/m² of uplift – the weight of the building has to hold it down, otherwise the basement can float up during construction.
How much does a 2.0 × 2.0 m pad footing on medium-dense sand settle under a load of about 1100 kN?
Foundation level −1.8 m, oedometer modulus of the sand E<sub>oed</sub> = 25 MPa, groundwater at −3.0 m.
Most students guess much more. Good sand is stiff: under a pad footing like this the settlement is less than two centimetres, and most of it comes from the first two metres below the base.
influence depth: Δσ<sub>z</sub> = 0.2 · σ′<sub>z0</sub> → m<sub>0</sub> ≈ 5.0 m
For the same footing, how deep below foundation level is the influence depth?
Where the additional stress drops to 20 % of the effective overburden stress.
Under a pad footing the stress spreads quickly: it is worth calculating down to about two and a half times the footing width. Under a wide raft, however, the influence depth is much deeper.
Δσ<sub>z</sub>(z) by Steinbrenner, below the centre of the footing
How much does a 3.1 m thick peat layer compress under an additional stress of 90 kPa?
Oedometer modulus of the peat: E<sub>oed</sub> = 0.8 MPa.

Thirty-five centimetres – many times the allowable value, and the peat keeps creeping for years afterwards. That is why a shallow foundation cannot be placed on peat: the load has to be carried through it by piles.
By what percentage does the volume of water increase when it freezes?
This is one cause of frost heave – the other is the growth of ice lenses.
Ice has about 9 % more volume than water. Yet most of the heave is caused by ice lenses: silty soil keeps drawing water up into the frozen zone, where it freezes into more ice.
ρ<sub>water</sub> ≈ 1000 kg/m³, ρ<sub>ice</sub> ≈ 917 kg/m³
What is the base resistance of an 80 cm diameter CFA pile whose base is 17 m deep in dense sandy gravel?
Illustrative unit base resistance at this depth: q<sub>b</sub> ≈ 5850 kPa.
About 300 tonnes on a single base of half a square metre. In a good bearing stratum the base carries most of the pile load – that is why the pile has to be embedded in the bearing stratum.
What active earth pressure acts on a 1 m length of a 6 m high wall in sand, with no groundwater?
About 11 tonnes on every metre run, and the pressure increases with depth: the lower third of the wall carries the most. Below the water table, water pressure is added, which can multiply the load.
Spot on
A perfect estimate by engineering standards.
Right ballpark
Within a factor of two – the order of magnitude is right.
Way off
Worth thinking about where the difference comes from.
